lesson.title: Dividing a World Neither Side Had Seen
lesson.summary: In 1494, Spain and Portugal drew a line across the Atlantic to settle their competing claims to newly encountered lands, a division that shaped where Spanish and Portuguese colonization would later take hold in the Americas.
lesson.body:
Christopher Columbus's 1492 voyage, undertaken for the Spanish crown, created an immediate diplomatic problem. Portugal had spent most of the fifteenth century building a network of trading posts along the African coast and had already secured papal recognition of its claims there. When Columbus returned describing islands across the Atlantic, Spain needed its own claim recognized before Portugal could contest it or claim the same territory first.

Spain moved quickly through the papacy. Pope Alexander VI, who was himself of Spanish origin, issued a series of bulls in 1493 that granted Spain rights to lands west of a line drawn about one hundred leagues west of the Azores and Cape Verde islands, with Portugal recognized as holding lands to the east. Portugal's King John II objected, arguing the line sat too close to his existing African holdings and left no room for further Portuguese exploration westward, which he suspected might reach valuable land.

Direct negotiation between the two crowns, rather than further papal arbitration, produced the actual settlement. Signed at the Spanish town of Tordesillas on June 7, 1494, the treaty moved the dividing line to three hundred seventy leagues west of the Cape Verde islands. Everything discovered west of that line would belong to Spain; everything east would belong to Portugal. Neither side had any accurate way to measure longitude at sea, so the line existed more as a diplomatic principle than a precise boundary, but it served its purpose of keeping the two Catholic Iberian powers from open war over new territory. Both crowns also agreed that any land already held by a Christian ruler before the treaty was signed would remain exempt from the division, a clause that mattered little in 1494 but showed how carefully the two sides tried to anticipate disputes.

The treaty's most visible consequence became clear six years later. In 1500, the Portuguese navigator Pedro Alvares Cabral, sailing toward the Indian Ocean, made landfall on the coast of present day Brazil, which happened to sit east of the Tordesillas line. That accident of geography gave Portugal a colony in South America and explains why Brazil speaks Portuguese today while the rest of Spanish America speaks Spanish.

The treaty had no force outside the two signatory kingdoms, and that limitation mattered enormously for the future of North America. England, France, and later the Dutch Republic never accepted a division of the world negotiated without them, and Protestant England in particular treated a papally sanctioned Catholic agreement as having no claim on English conscience or ambition. When John Cabot sailed for Henry VII and later English explorers pushed toward North America, they were acting on exactly this refusal to be bound by Tordesillas, setting up the competing European claims that would define colonization north of Spanish Florida. The line's legacy still shows on a modern map of the Americas, visible in the linguistic and cultural boundary that separates Portuguese speaking Brazil from its Spanish speaking neighbors.
